1:
That the departure was known in advance, and widely, is agreed by everyone who touches it. Clarke has it revealed not only to Elijah but to Elisha and to the schools at Bethel and Jericho, so that all were expecting it. Keil and Delitzsch add that the disciples were told to strengthen their faith, and Wesley has it revealed to some of the sons of the prophets and by them to the whole college. Gill infers Elijah's own foreknowledge from his movements under divine direction, and Henry leaves open whether the sons of the prophets learned it from Elijah, by the spirit of prophecy among themselves, or from the solemnity of his farewell. Henry alone asks why the honour fell to Elijah, and answers by looking back on his services, down on a degenerate church needing proof of another life, and forward to the ascension of Christ, of which this was a type.

Why Elijah kept urging his companion to stay behind is the first real dispute. Gill offers three possibilities: modesty about the honour coming to him, a wish to spare Elisha the grief of parting, or a test of whether Elisha knew and how much he cared. Clarke narrows it to humility or a trial of fidelity, and Henry to humility or, as he prefers, a trial that would make the adherence more commendable, comparing Naomi urging Ruth to turn back. Wesley adds a fourth, that Elijah might be left alone to prepare for his change, while allowing the others and observing that God's honour required witnesses of so glorious a translation. Ellicott rejects the whole line: it was said neither to test Elisha's affection nor out of a modesty that would keep him from seeing the ascension, but because Elijah did not know whether it was God's will that Elisha should come, and the threefold refusal settled the doubt.

The route is given more precision by Ellicott than by the rest. He identifies the Gilgal of this verse as the one in Ephraim, on a hill south-west of Shiloh, taking the name to mean the Ring and belonging to more than one place, and argues from the words they went down that the Gilgal near Jordan cannot be meant. On why Bethel, he sets aside Ewald's reason, that Elijah wished to see once more the spiritual centre of the northern kingdom, for the business of confirming the prophetic guilds, which Bähr suggests were planted at these old sanctuaries to counteract the illegal worship at its headquarters. Wesley agrees on the errand and remarks that the answer given was truth but not the whole truth, the journey being far longer than Bethel. Henry and Gill both dwell on the schools themselves, Henry holding that these colleges supplied what Israel lacked in priests and temple service and so kept religion alive in a time of general apostasy.

Two phrases are then construed closely. On the taking of Elijah from above his head, Keil and Delitzsch read a pictorial expression for his being raised from Elisha's side, comparing the words used of the ascension in Acts. Ellicott lists three possibilities and ranks them: the word may stand for the person, or it may mean from his position of superiority as master and teacher, or, very improbably, it may refer literally to a departure over Elisha's head. On the order to be silent they agree about the tone and differ about the reason. Henry says it was not spoken peevishly but by a man composed himself and wanting them composed, and Wesley has him asking not to have his grief aggravated. Ellicott denies both that it was to prevent a crowd and that it guarded his master's modesty, making it simply that the subject was painful to them both, and notes that the Hebrew word imitates the sound of hushing.
4:
The exact repetition of the exchange at each stage is turned to account differently by two voices. Ellicott takes it as evidence of transmission, the language of the Bethel scene recurring word for word at Jericho and at Jordan because the narrative was first handed on by oral tradition, probably within the prophetic guilds at the local sanctuaries. Keil and Delitzsch look instead for a purpose in the route: Elijah did not merely touch at Gilgal, Bethel and Jericho because they lay on his way to the river, but for the same reason that his ascension had been revealed beforehand at those places. Gill notes in passing what the itinerary implies about Jericho, a city lately rebuilt under a curse on its builder and yet blessed with a school of the prophets, and reads Elijah's repeated urging as a man seemingly anxious to be rid of his companion before the event. Ellicott borrows from Reuss a description of the whole mood: all the disciples have a presentiment of their loss, they tell each other their fears and Elisha will not let the sorrow run free, a respectful silence and a resignation not free of foreboding suiting the case, Elisha clinging to his master as if he could hold him back while the disciples follow them with their eyes; and the monotony of the successive scenes, Reuss observes, adds to the solemnity of the whole.

Why fifty of them followed is answered four ways, and the answers differ in how much they allow to curiosity. Gill has them wanting a view of the assumption and to be witnesses of it. Wesley says expressly that it was not to satisfy curiosity but so that they might testify of it to others. Clarke infers from their expectation that they could have learned of it only from Elijah himself or by direct revelation. Ellicott is the most concrete: they took their stand directly opposite the place where the two men halted, though at a distance behind, because they wanted to see whether and how their master would get across at a point where there was no ford.

What the garment was interests three of the voices. Gill reports the opinion that it was not the hairy garment but a shorter robe worn on the shoulders, while noting that the Greek renders it by a word which, on Isidore's account, means a goat's skin hanging from the neck and girt at the loins, and suggesting that such clothing may be why Elijah was called a hairy man. Clarke follows the Greek in making it a sheep-skin, explains that skins dressed with the hair on were the simple insignia of a prophet's or priest's office, and traces the custom down to the lamb's skin hood worn by certain university graduates and the ermine on royal robes. Ellicott keeps it the hairy mantle that marked him as prophet, comparing the mantle of hair in Zechariah, and rejects the head-dress of the Syriac and Arabic. On the smiting itself they converge. Keil and Delitzsch make the cloak, the outward sign of the office, the vehicle of the power, and Ellicott sets the act beside Moses smiting the rock and stretching his rod over the sea, the visible sign being made the channel of an invisible force. Clarke calls it a most astonishing miracle possible only to the almighty power of God. Wesley adds the typology, that these waters had once yielded to the ark and now to the mantle, which served those who lacked the ark as an equivalent token of God's presence, and that death is the Jordan God's children must pass through, divided for them by the death of Christ.
9:
The offer itself is read as a father's parting act. Ellicott takes Elijah to be doing what a dying father does, blessing his spiritual son before departing, and connects it with the cry that follows at the ascension. Henry has him moved by the constancy of Elisha's attendance, and borrows from Bishop Hall the observation that he does not say ask of me when I am gone, as though he would be better able to befriend his servant from heaven, but ask before I go: friends on earth can be spoken to and can answer, where we know of no access to any friend in heaven but Christ. Henry also marks what Elisha did not ask for, neither wealth nor honour nor exemption from trouble but a fitness for service, and notices the form of the request, let it be upon me rather than give it me.

What the double portion means is settled the same way by four voices and contested by the fifth. Clarke grounds it in the law of the firstborn, who received a double share of all his father's goods: Elisha reckoned himself the firstborn among men who were called the sons of a teacher, and claimed accordingly twice what any other disciple would have, the Hebrew meaning rather two parts than twice the quantity. Ellicott says the same and states the alternative in order to reject it, that the words do not mean give me twice as great a share of the spirit of prophecy as thou hast thyself, as many have wrongly interpreted, but make me thy true spiritual heir; Henry and Wesley both put it as double to what the rest of the prophets had rather than double to Elijah's own measure. Keil and Delitzsch catalogue the misreading instead, tracing it from Ephraem Syrus down to Köster and Krummacher and through Luther's following of the Latin, with others referring it to the greater number of Elisha's miracles or to the gifts of prophecy. Wesley alone separates the asking from the outcome, holding that God gave more than was desired or expected, so that Elisha seems to have had a greater portion of the Spirit's gifts than Elijah himself.

Why the thing asked was hard they answer in two different registers. Gill makes it rarity, a privilege seldom enjoyed and hard to obtain, few being so favoured of God. Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all make it a question of power rather than of frequency: it was not in Elijah's gift at all but in God's only, so that calling it hard was a disclaimer. Henry takes the word as pedagogy, that by calling it hard Elijah taught his servant to value it, those being best prepared for spiritual blessings who are most sensible of their worth and of their own unworthiness to receive them.

The condition attached is where the readings part company. Clarke will not let it rest on the bare act of seeing, since a divine gift could not depend on whether a man's eye caught the moment, and takes it to mean no more than that Elisha should continue with him until the translation. Ellicott, quoting Thenius, makes it a test of worthiness, that if the Lord thought him worthy to witness the departure he would be worthy of the boon, and finds implied in it that the departure would be something above the perception of ordinary men. Wesley reads the sign as a spur, proposed under the Spirit's direction so as to engage Elisha to wait more earnestly and pray more fervently. Henry holds both halves at once, making close attendance to the last both the condition and the means of obtaining the spirit asked for, since the comforts and experiences of departing saints steel the resolutions of those who watch them; and he allows that it may have been meant only as a token.
11:
How literally the fiery chariot is to be taken divides the voices as sharply as anything in the chapter. Wesley takes it at full strength: the angels appeared in that form, and where the faithful are carried invisibly into Abraham's bosom, Elijah had his body to carry with him, so the guard was visible, and not in human shape, though they might have borne him in their arms, but as chariot and horses, that he might ride in state and in triumph like a prince. Clarke insists on the plain sense for a different reason, to shut out Priestley's conjecture that Enoch, Elijah and Christ, having no relation to another world, must be in this one; the text says Elijah went up into heaven, and Scripture places our Lord at the right hand of the Majesty on high. Keil and Delitzsch take a middle course, making it a tempest accompanied by a fiery phenomenon which appeared to Elisha's eyes as a chariot of fire with horses of fire. Ellicott argues the other way at length. The word means a storm-blast, and the Hebrew mind saw God working in the terrific phenomena of nature, the storm-cloud his chariot and the thunder his voice, so that we must be cautious of too literal a sense: the essential meaning is that God suddenly took Elijah to himself amid a grand display of power through natural forces, and the popular conception of a fiery car drawn by horses, as in Blake's picture, is read into the text rather than gathered from it. He reports Bähr's suggestion that the verb here means disappeared or was consumed, quotes Von Gerlach that Scripture leaves unanswered all questions of whither and where and what change, and adds that the ascension of Elijah is nowhere alluded to in the rest of the Bible.

The cry that follows is agreed to have two halves. Ellicott puts it plainly: the first words say what Elijah was to Elisha, the second what he was to the nation. On the second all four voices reach the same paraphrase from different directions. Keil and Delitzsch make chariot and horsemen, the things on which Israel's kings rested the security of the kingdom, a figure for the defence Elijah's ministry had been. Clarke and Ellicott both quote the Targum, that he was of more use to Israel by his intercession than horses and chariots were, and Ellicott adds the force of the figure in that age, when chariots and horsemen were the chief military arm and indispensable against the Aramean states. Clarke brings in the later Jewish book that makes the fiery horses an emblem of the prophet's burning zeal, who stood up as fire and whose word burned as a lamp. On the first half Keil and Delitzsch call Elijah his spiritual father, who had begotten him through the word of God, and Wesley speaks of fatherly affection and authority together, the scholars of the prophets being called sons, so that Elisha saw his own case as a fatherless child's and lamented it. Wesley alone ties the second half to what had just been seen, taking the words to allude to the very form of chariot and horses that had passed before his eyes.

The close of the scene is read briefly and in agreement. Keil and Delitzsch, Clarke and Ellicott all take the rending of the clothes from top to bottom as the measure of an extreme sorrow, Clarke adding that it was for the loss of so good and glorious a master. Gill looks at what the seeing secured rather than what the parting cost: Elisha had now the token by which he might expect the double portion, and the whole scene answers closely to the ascension of Christ, after which the disciples had their own extraordinary effusion of the Spirit.
13:
The fallen mantle is read by everyone as a credential. Gill has Elijah with no further use for it and Elisha in need of it, having just torn his own clothes, and makes its coming into his hands the token that he succeeded to the office. Keil and Delitzsch put the same thing in two directions at once, a pledge to Elisha that his request was granted and a visible sign to others that he was the divinely appointed successor. Wesley has God so ordering the fall for Elisha's comfort and the strengthening of his faith, and adds that Elijah was gone where he needed no mantle to adorn him, to shelter him from weather or to wrap his face in. Henry makes the exchange explicit: Elijah did not let fall his body as other men do but let fall his mantle instead, being unclothed that he might be clothed with immortality, and the legacy, of small value in itself, was worth more than thousands in gold as a token of the Spirit's descent. He adds the caution that Elisha took it up not as a relic to be worshipped but as a garment to be worn,.

The words Elisha speaks over the water are taken as faith rather than complaint. Ellicott paraphrases them as asking whether God has left the earth with his prophet, and if not, that he would now show his power and make good the granting of the request; he calls the form a sort of irony of faith, Elisha seeking the Lord as the only source of power, and compares the prophet who blames priests and people for running to idols instead of asking where the Lord is. Henry marks what the question does not say: not where is Elijah, as a man poring on his loss, but where is the God of Elijah.

The doubled clause about smiting the water is the chapter's hardest textual knot, and four solutions are on offer. Clarke reports the Latin, which makes it two strikings, the first failing to divide the river, perhaps because Elisha confided too much in his own strength, and the second succeeding after he had invoked the God of Elijah; he then takes the reading apart, since no other version follows the distinction and the clause saying the waters did not divide is nowhere in the Hebrew. Ellicott says outright that something is wrong here, notes that the Greek copies the two Hebrew words instead of translating them, and canvasses the alternatives: Keil joins them to the question, giving where is the God of Elijah, even he, which Thenius thinks a doubtful use and would replace by Houbigant's correction yielding where then; Ellicott himself suggests either that the original repeated the word where for emphasis, or that the words should be transposed to give and he smote, he also, like Elijah. The Latin rendering he treats as an old attempt to account for the twofold smiting rather than as evidence.

What the crossing established is Henry's subject. Having parted from his father, Elisha returns to his sons in the schools, with Jordan between; the river had divided to make way for Elijah to his glory, and he will try whether it divides to make way for him to his work, and by that know that God is with him and the double portion his. Elijah's last miracle becomes Elisha's first, so that he begins where his master left off and there is no vacancy; and he uses the mantle as Elijah had used it, to signify that he meant to keep to his master's methods and introduce nothing new, unlike those who think themselves wiser than their predecessors. Henry draws a general lesson from the garment, that the remains of great and good men, their sayings and writings and examples, ought to be gathered up by those who survive them.
15:
Who the watchers were is left open by the one voice that asks. Ellicott cannot tell whether these are the fifty who had stood opposite at a distance or not, and concludes on the whole that the whole guild residing at Jericho is meant, assembled at the river to await Elisha's return and so witnesses of the miracle. Clarke takes the fifty strong men offered for the search to be the same fifty who had seen Elijah taken up, and Gill thinks the speakers meant themselves, being young and able to travel for days. Ellicott suggests rather that they were attendants on the guild, and notes that their being men of valour mattered because a search in the mountains carried danger. On what the watchers inferred there is no dispute. Clarke calls it a natural conclusion from seeing Elisha with the mantle and working the same miracle, and Ellicott says the proof was simply that he had just repeated his master's act. Wesley draws out what the homage cost them: they had been trained in the schools and Elisha had been taken from the plough, yet seeing God with him they submitted to him as their head, as the people did to Joshua when Moses was dead, which he turns into a rule that those who evidently have God's presence deserve our esteem whatever the meanness of their extraction and education.

Why they wanted to search at all is answered three ways, and the answers matter for how the ascension itself is understood. Keil and Delitzsch put it down to simple incapacity: they could not realise the fact of the translation, although it had been revealed to them beforehand. Clarke supposes they allowed that Elijah had gone up but thought the Spirit might have come down with him and set him on some remote mountain or valley. Wesley offers two possibilities, that God had taken him only for a time, or that only his soul was taken and the body cast down somewhere, which they wished to find and bury honourably. Ellicott rejects that second motive by name, since Keil proposes it and since the disciples plainly expected to find Elijah alive, and he reports a Greek reading that has the Spirit cast him into the Jordan, which if authentic would mean they thought him hidden among the reeds of the bank to escape some danger. He then presses the point he had made at the ascension itself: this request is a good comment on those verses, and shows that what is told there is certainly not that Elijah rode visibly into heaven in a fiery car, whatever the popular notion.

The phrase for Elisha's yielding is rendered four ways. Gill and Wesley both take it of shame at refusing them any longer, Wesley adding the motive, lest they should think the refusal came of neglect for his master or contempt for them. Clarke makes it the awkwardness of a man who sees that nothing but the search will satisfy them and cannot decently hold out. Ellicott gives the Hebrew as being embarrassed, disconcerted, put out of countenance, and sets beside it Thenius, who would have them carry their importunity to a shameless length, and Keil and Bähr, who make it disappointment in the hope of dissuading them. With the return of the searchers the history of Elijah closes, and Ellicott marks the close with two quotations: Reuss, that when the prophet withdrew the providence guiding Israel did not forsake the people, a portion of his spirit passing to his disciples, who are forbidden to seek their master in the desert and must find among themselves the means of carrying on his work; and Thenius, who takes the whole section for a distinct fragment of a lost history of Elijah, a judgment Ellicott passes on with a question mark against the word poetical.
19:
Who brought the complaint is itself disputed. Ellicott insists that it was the citizens and not the sons of the prophets who put the new prophet's powers to this trial; Henry reports the opinion that the barren part was precisely where the sons of the prophets lodged, and that these are the men of the city meant. What the complaint was raises a larger question. Clarke takes it simply, the barrenness of the ground being the effect of the badness of the water, and Wesley allows either an original barrenness or one inflicted by the curse on the man who rebuilt the city. Ellicott denies that the soil is in question at all: the following verse shows the waters to be the cause, the word rendered ground stands for the land's inhabitants and their animals, and the sense is that the country bears dead births or suffers many miscarriages, so that barren land is an incorrect translation. He adds that this is not the popular superstition Reuss takes it for.

The means chosen divide the voices along the same line. Gill has the vessel new so that none could think the virtue lay in anything previously in it, Wesley so that no legal pollution might hinder the work. Ellicott makes the newness fit a purpose needing an uncontaminated instrument, and parts company with the rest on the salt, calling it an antiseptic and so an appropriate sacramental medium for a divine influence that was to expel the spring's corruption. Wesley holds the opposite, that salt is a most improper remedy since it makes water brackish and land barren, and was chosen to show that the thing was done solely by divine power, which can work without means or against them. Clarke agrees and quotes Jarchi for it, that salt corrupts water and the miracle is therefore evident; he adds that any natural tendency in the salt could have acted only briefly and on the water then rising, where this cure was permanent. Henry reasons from quantity, that so small a measure could do nothing and the new cruse add nothing, the point being that those who would be helped must be employed and have their faith tried.

Where the salt went matters to all of them. Clarke notes that he cast it where the water sprang out of the earth, and Ellicott identifies the place with the spring that still irrigates the plain. Henry draws the moral from the location: the spring was treated and so the streams and the ground they watered were healed, which is how lives are reformed, by renewing hearts. On the authority claimed, Henry and Ellicott agree exactly. Neither the prophet's own power nor the natural virtue of the salt did it but the creative will of God, and Henry adds that a kindness done with a thus saith the Lord would make the townsmen readier to take reproof with the same preface.

How far the cure lasted is read narrowly by one voice and widely by another. Ellicott takes unto this day to mean the time when the narrative was first written down. Gill carries it much further: the waters remained sweet to Josephus's time and to his own, there being a spring still called Elisha's fountain, received, as Maundrell describes it, in a basin some nine or ten paces long and dividing into streams that make the whole field fruitful; and he notes that other travellers call the water clear and cool while Pliny names it the beautiful stream and calls it hot and medicinal. Henry sets the miracle in the city's history: Jericho was built in disobedience and at the cost of the builder's children, yet was never ordered demolished nor closed to God's people, so that within walls raised by iniquity there grew up a nursery of piety.
23:
The errand to Bethel is agreed. Gill has Elisha go up from Jericho in the plain to the town on its hill to tell the sons of the prophets of the assumption and confirm his standing in his master's room; Wesley adds what the place was, the mother-city of idolatry, where the prophets had planted themselves to bear witness against it with small success. Ellicott calls it the chief seat of the illicit worship.

Who the mockers were, and what they meant, is where the voices separate. All three who discuss the word deny that small children are meant. Clarke argues it from usage, the same term being applied to Isaac at twenty-eight, to Joseph at thirty-nine and to the young men of the princes of the provinces who were soldiers, and concludes that the mockers were accountable for their conduct. Ellicott allows any age between six or seven and twenty, reasoning that little children would neither hit on a biting sarcasm nor sally out in a body. Wesley simply takes them for young men old enough to discern good from evil. On the taunt itself Clarke and Wesley agree and Ellicott dissents. Clarke reads it as blasphemy, an invitation to ascend as it was pretended the master had, and Wesley gives it as asking why the servant did not follow his friend to heaven. Ellicott denies the reference: the Bethelites knew no more of the ascension than the prophets of Jericho did, and the word plainly refers to what Elisha was doing at that moment, going up the steep road slowly in a mantle that drew attention. On its second half they converge again, Clarke rendering it empty skull, Wesley calling the mockery of a natural infirmity a great sin, and Ellicott noting that baldness was a reproach and suspect as a mark of leprosy, Elisha perhaps being bald prematurely.

Whether the curse can be defended is taken up directly by two voices. Keil and Delitzsch meet the charge of immorality head on: if it were established it would not touch Elisha only but fall back on the Lord, who executed his servant's curse in that manner; and they refuse the expedient of a plot got up by the city's rulers with the children put forward, since it is enough that the spirit prevailing in Bethel showed itself openly in the mockery. Clarke shifts the agency instead: Elisha did not destroy them and had no power to bring bears out of the wood, so the thing was either accident or divine judgment, and if judgment then God was its sole author and the curse only declaratory of what he was about to do. Ellicott quotes Keil for the opposite view, that the curse avenged the honour of God violated in his person.

Clarke alone offers a reconstruction of his own, and it turns on the detail of the species. He asks whether these forty-two may not have been young men who had been in the wood destroying the whelps of these same she-bears, which now followed and tore them for the injury; the mention of she-bears gives the conjecture some colour, and on that reading the beasts were made ready by their loss to execute the curse while God's justice guided them to the spot, so that a natural effect appears as a divine cause. Gill keeps to the scene: Elisha turned with a stern countenance to shame them,, to no purpose. On the journey that ends the chapter the voices agree and differ only in emphasis. Gill notes that Carmel was Elijah's old haunt and reckons the distance fifty-six miles. Keil and Delitzsch have him go there to strengthen himself in solitude for his master's work, and Ellicott to cultivate his master's memory in caves well suited to concealment, both ending him at Samaria, where he kept his permanent house.
